source.title: Core Knowledge Deficits in Multi-Modal Language Models
source.authors: Yi-Jiang Li; Qing-Ying Gao; Tianwei Zhao; Bing-Yang Wang; Hao-Ran Sun; Haiyun Lyu; Robert D. Hawkins; Nuno Vasconcelos; Tal Golan; Dezhi Luo; Ho-Kin Deng

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figures and tables are flattened in the text, but the relevant scaling results are also described in prose.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures benchmark-task performance across differently sized multimodal models and reports how performance changes with size. This is a different measure and setting from held-out language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: Only the paper's own model-size versus benchmark-performance results are included. Scaling laws for loss and compute cited from other studies are not results of this study; it does not test loss scaling, extrapolation from small runs, or compute-optimal allocation.
record.test_reason: The study regresses CoreCognition benchmark accuracy on log parameter count across about 219 heterogeneous existing MLLMs (Sec. 4.4, Fig. 7). That bears on V6, downstream improvement with scale, in a new setting: multimodal models compared across families rather than controlled runs. It reports linear slopes per ability rather than a predictive fit, so it is closer to T3 than T2. It does not measure pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that scaling mainly benefits high-level (Formal Operational) abilities, while its effect on low-level core abilities is limited, absent or even negative (perspective-taking), so model size alone is insufficient for core knowledge. They add that larger models show persistent core deficits or more shortcut-taking rather than moving toward genuine understanding.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates multimodal benchmark accuracy across existing models and estimates linear-regression slopes; it does not measure held-out language-model loss across controlled pretraining runs.

fits_no_version.finding: Reasoning or test-time-scaled models show no significant gain over their instruction-tuned counterparts on 10 of 12 abilities, and perform worse on perspective-taking (P=0.0037).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Test-time or reasoning scaling does not improve core perceptual abilities in MLLMs.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The scaling analysis is across heterogeneous existing models rather than controlled runs. Exact slope values are not given in the prose, and the paper states that it does not analyze scaling after partitioning by prompt type or model competence.
record.rows_left_out: No additional own results directly testing the listed versions were identified. Other findings on concept hacking concern controlled label manipulations, not performance scaling under the conditions named by these versions.

untested.parts: Whether improvement is predictable: no extrapolation and no reported fit quality. Performance as a function of pretraining loss. Controlled scaling within one training recipe, since models differ in data, architecture and vision encoder.
All parts; no pretraining loss is measured.
All parts; the study is multimodal but measures benchmark accuracy, not loss power laws.

missing.what: The scaling-effect pattern replicates in all three input-format subgroups (single image, single image/video, multi-frame). It is not analysed by prompt or model competence.
Susceptibility to concept hacking (control vs manipulation accuracy) does not correlate simply with model size; large models such as GPT-4o show shortcut reliance.

record.verdict_notes: The scaling analysis is a cross-model linear regression of accuracy on log parameters. Models are heterogeneous in training data, architecture and recipe, and parameter counts for proprietary models are unknown, which plausibly explains 219 rather than 230 models. This is a weak test of predictable scaling, so the labels apply only to the direction and relative size of the slopes. Tranche changed from T2 to T3: a new setting (MLLMs on a core-cognition benchmark) rather than a different method on the original question.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether loss power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation, and its dependence on compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
The study tests performance across model sizes on its benchmark, but does not test performance as a function of pretraining loss.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices, and whether loss curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: 219 MLLMs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Linear regression of benchmark performance against model size; scaling effect estimated as the regression slope.

conditions.value: seven of nine low-level abilities in Sensorimotor and Concrete Operational stages

rows.measure: CoreCognition accuracy scaling with model size
rows.value: Significantly less improvement with increasing size than higher-level abilities
rows.uncertainty: 95% CI shown in Fig. 7; numerical intervals not stated
rows.note: Aggregate result reported for seven of nine low-level abilities; the paper does not give their individual slope values in the prose.
rows.check: The link and state are fine. The value is relative: 'significantly less improvement' than Formal Operational abilities, with no slopes given in the prose. The abstract says 'reduced, or even absent, scalability', so some of these seven abilities may be near zero, but they cannot be told apart from the text. Subject count: 219 models after filtering, not 230.

rows.subject: MLLMs (aggregate; Formal Operational abilities)
rows.operation_detail: Linear regression of benchmark performance against model size; scaling effect estimated as the regression slope.
rows.measure: CoreCognition accuracy scaling with model size
rows.uncertainty: 95% CI shown in Fig. 7; numerical intervals not stated
rows.note: The paper describes the high-level abilities as benefiting from scaling, in contrast to the low-level abilities.
rows.check: The baseline should be the low-level abilities (r1), not 'not stated'. Only the slope direction is reported; no slope value or fit quality is given.

rows.subject: MLLMs (aggregate; perspective-taking ability)
rows.operation_detail: Linear regression of benchmark performance against model size; scaling effect estimated as the regression slope.
rows.measure: CoreCognition accuracy scaling with model size
rows.uncertainty: 95% CI shown in Fig. 7; numerical intervals not stated
rows.note: The authors describe perspective-taking as having an inverse scaling trend.
rows.check: This is correct: perspective-taking 'even declines with scale' (Fig. 7, bottom right). No slope magnitude is given in the text.

relationships.condition: Formal Operational abilities (intentionality, mechanical reasoning, tool use), across about 219 MLLMs from 1B to 110B
relationships.reason: The authors state that scaling primarily benefits high-level reasoning, with positive regression slopes (r2).
relationships.display_finding: Positive regression slopes associated larger models with better intentionality, mechanical reasoning, and tool use.

relationships.condition: Seven of nine Sensorimotor and Concrete Operational abilities (excluding hierarchy and perceptual constancy)
relationships.reason: These abilities improve significantly less with size than Formal Operational ones; the authors call the gains limited or absent (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Seven of nine abilities showed limited or absent gains and improved significantly less with size than Formal Operational abilities.

relationships.reason: Accuracy declines as parameter count grows, which the authors call an inverse scaling trend (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy decreased as parameter scale increased.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
